claim: Metabolic disorders are highly prevalent in modern society.
source: Metabolic disorders are highly prevalent in modern society.
evidence: This is a general statement about the prevalence of metabolic disorders, supported by the citation to Hoehn et al., 2010 in the Introduction.

claim: Exercise mimetics are defined as pharmacological compounds that can produce the beneficial effects of fitness.
source: Exercise mimetics are defined as pharmacological compounds that can produce the beneficial effects of fitness.
evidence: This is a definition statement supported by citation to Fan and Evans, 2017.

claim: Eugenol improved endurance capacity in mice.
source: Here, we showed that eugenol improved endurance capacity, caused the conversion of fast-to-slow muscle fibers, and promoted white fat browning and lipolysis in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased exhaustion time in EUG100 group (Figure 2A).

claim: Eugenol caused the conversion of fast-to-slow muscle fibers in mice.
source: Here, we showed that eugenol improved endurance capacity, caused the conversion of fast-to-slow muscle fibers, and promoted white fat browning and lipolysis in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing changes in MyHC expression (Figure 1D, E, G) and muscle color (Figure 1C).

claim: Eugenol promoted white fat browning and lipolysis in mice.
source: Here, we showed that eugenol improved endurance capacity, caused the conversion of fast-to-slow muscle fibers, and promoted white fat browning and lipolysis in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing changes in fat tissue weight, gene expression, and protein expression (Figure 3).

claim: Eugenol promoted muscle fiber-type transformation by activating TRPV1-mediated CaN signaling pathway.
source: Mechanistically, eugenol promoted muscle fiber-type transformation by activating TRPV1-mediated CaN signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that TRPV1 and CaN inhibition blocked eugenol's effects (Figure 5).

claim: IL-15 is a myokine that is regulated by the CaN/NFATc1 signaling pathway.
source: Subsequently, we identified IL-15 as a myokine that is regulated by the CaN/nuclear factor of activated T cells cytoplasmic 1 (NFATc1) signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Ca2+ ionophore and CsA effects on IL-15 expression (Figure 7), EMSA results, and luciferase assays.

claim: TRPV1-mediated CaN/NFATc1 signaling, activated by eugenol, controlled IL-15 levels in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Moreover, we found that TRPV1-mediated CaN/NFATc1 signaling, activated by eugenol, controlled IL-15 levels in C2C12 myotubes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that TRPV1 and CaN inhibition blocked eugenol's effects on IL-15 (Figure 9C, D).

claim: Eugenol may act as an exercise mimetic to improve metabolic health via activating the TRPV1-mediated CaN signaling pathway.
source: Our results suggest that eugenol may act as an exercise mimetic to improve metabolic health via activating the TRPV1-mediated CaN signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Due to the lack of regular exercise among many individuals, metabolic diseases are highly prevalent in modern society.
source: Due to the lack of regular exercise among many individuals (Carlson et al., 2010), metabolic diseases are highly prevalent in modern society (Hoehn et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2010 and Hoehn et al., 2010.

claim: Some synthetic exercise mimetics such as AICAR, GW501516, SRT1720, and GSK4716 have been used to improve fitness.
source: Although some synthetic exercise mimetics such as AICAR (AMPK activator), GW501516 (PPARδ activator), SRT1720 (SIRT1 activator), and GSK4716 (ERRγ activator) have been used to improve fitness (Feige et al., 2008; Narkar et al., 2008; Rangwala et al., 2010), the safety and health of each drug must be considered.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feige et al., 2008; Narkar et al., 2008; Rangwala et al., 2010.

claim: Plant extracts such as resveratrol, lycium barbarum, and epicatechin have demonstrated potential as a new class of low-toxin exercise mimetics.
source: In recent years, plant extracts such as resveratrol, lycium barbarum, and epicatechin have demonstrated potential as a new class of low-toxin exercise mimetics (Meng et al., 2020; Nogueira et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meng et al., 2020; Nogueira et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2020.

claim: Muscle fibers are commonly divided into slow oxidative fibers and fast glycolytic/oxidative fibers based on their metabolism and contractile properties.
source: Based on their metabolism and contractile properties, muscle fibers are commonly divided into slow oxidative fibers (muscle fibers that express myosin heavy chain (MyHC) I) and fast glycolytic/oxidative fibers (muscle fibers that express MyHC IIa, MyHC IIx, or MyHC IIb) (Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011).
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by citation to Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011.

claim: Different muscle fibers exhibit a high degree of plasticity and are regulated by exercise.
source: Different muscle fibers exhibit a high degree of plasticity and are regulated by exercise (Egan and Zierath, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Egan and Zierath, 2013.

claim: The increased proportion of slow muscle fibers contributes to the enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and lipid metabolism.
source: The increased proportion of slow muscle fibers contributes to the enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and lipid metabolism (Carlson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carlson et al., 2010.

claim: One of the benefits of exercise is to treat metabolic disorders by promoting slow muscle fiber remodeling.
source: Therefore, one of the benefits of exercise is to treat metabolic disorders by promoting slow muscle fiber remodeling (Duan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duan et al., 2017.

claim: Myokines are defined as cytokines or peptides that are released from skeletal muscle cells, which exert autocrine, paracrine, or endocrine effects.
source: Myokines are defined as cytokines or peptides that are released from skeletal muscle cells, which exert autocrine, paracrine, or endocrine effects (Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012).
evidence: This is a definition statement supported by citation to Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012.

claim: Myokines exert systemic regulation of exercise by acting on the muscle, fat, liver, pancreas, and other organs, effectively improving insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic disorders of type 2 diabetes.
source: As a medium of crosstalk between muscles and other organs, myokines exert systemic regulation of exercise by acting on the muscle, fat, liver, pancreas, and other organs, effectively improving insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic disorders of type 2 diabetes (Severinsen and Pedersen, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Severinsen and Pedersen, 2020.

claim: Eugenol is a safe natural compound extracted from clove oil and various plant spices such as basil, bay leaves, and cinnamon.
source: Eugenol is a safe natural compound extracted from clove oil and various plant spices such as basil, bay leaves, and cinnamon (Kaur et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaur et al., 2010.

claim: Eugenol exhibits antioxidative, antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer activities.
source: Eugenol exhibits a variety of biological activities, including antioxidative (Magalhães et al., 2019), antibacterial (Devi et al., 2010), anti-inflammatory (Magalhães et al., 2019), and anti-cancer activities (Lesgards et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magalhães et al., 2019; Devi et al., 2010; Lesgards et al., 2014.

claim: Eugenol could be a promising therapeutic drug for preventing diabetes and obesity.
source: Recent studies have also suggested that eugenol could be a promising therapeutic drug for preventing diabetes and obesity (Al Trad et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2012; Mnafgui et al., 2013; Srinivasan et al., 2014), indicating its potential as an exercise mimetic.
evidence: Supported by citations to Al Trad et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2012; Mnafgui et al., 2013; Srinivasan et al., 2014.

claim: TRPV1 has been reported to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism.
source: In addition, as a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family, TRP vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), also known as the capsaicin receptor, has been reported to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism (Luo et al., 2012), counter obesity (Baskaran et al., 2016), and intervene diabetes (Wang et al., 2012), making it a potential target protein for discovering exercise mimetics.
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2012.

claim: TRPV1 has been reported to counter obesity.
source: In addition, as a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family, TRP vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), also known as the capsaicin receptor, has been reported to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism (Luo et al., 2012), counter obesity (Baskaran et al., 2016), and intervene diabetes (Wang et al., 2012), making it a potential target protein for discovering exercise mimetics.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baskaran et al., 2016.

claim: TRPV1 has been reported to intervene diabetes.
source: In addition, as a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family, TRP vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), also known as the capsaicin receptor, has been reported to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism (Luo et al., 2012), counter obesity (Baskaran et al., 2016), and intervene diabetes (Wang et al., 2012), making it a potential target protein for discovering exercise mimetics.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Eugenol contains a vanilloyl fragment that may bind to TRPV1 similarly to capsaicin.
source: Eugenol contains a vanilloyl fragment that may bind to TRPV1 similarly to capsaicin, implying that eugenol might exert its biological activity via TRPV1 (Harb et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harb et al., 2019 and molecular structure knowledge.

claim: Eugenol activates TRPV1 in a heterologous expression system and rat trigeminal ganglion neurons.
source: It has been found that eugenol activates TRPV1 in a heterologous expression system and rat trigeminal ganglion neurons (Xu et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xu et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003.

claim: Eugenol activated TRPV1 in skeletal muscle.
source: Furthermore, a recent study demonstrated that eugenol activated TRPV1 in skeletal muscle (Jiang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2022.

claim: TRPV1 is an important Ca2+ entry pathway contributing to increase intracellular Ca2+.
source: TRPV1 is an important Ca2+ entry pathway contributing to increase intracellular Ca2+ (Nilius et al., 2007), suggesting that TRPV1 may regulate many biological processes through Ca2+-dependent signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nilius et al., 2007.

claim: Calcineurin is a core signaling to promote fast-to-slow muscle fiber transformation.
source: As a Ca2+-dependent signaling, calcineurin (CaN) is a core signaling to promote fast-to-slow muscle fiber transformation (Sakuma and Yamaguchi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakuma and Yamaguchi, 2010.

claim: CaN signaling plays an essential role in regulating the expression of myokine IL-6.
source: Additionally, CaN signaling plays an essential role in regulating the expression of myokine IL-6 (Banzet et al., 2005; Banzet et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banzet et al., 2005; Banzet et al., 2007.

claim: Eugenol did not have any effect on the body weight in mice.
source: As depicted in Figure 1A and B, eugenol did not have any effect on the body weight or skeletal muscle weight in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Eugenol did not have any effect on skeletal muscle weight in mice.
source: As depicted in Figure 1A and B, eugenol did not have any effect on the body weight or skeletal muscle weight in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The skeletal muscle in the EUG50 and EUG100 groups exhibited a redder muscle color.
source: However, the skeletal muscle in the EUG50 and EUG100 groups exhibited a redder muscle color (Figure 1C), indicating a shift from fast-to-slow muscle fiber in these two groups.
evidence: Supported by visual observation in Figure 1C.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 increased the expression of slow MyHC in gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior muscles.
source: Further experiments showed that EUG50 and EUG100 increased the expression of slow MyHC and decreased the expression of fast MyHC protein in gastrocnemius (GAS) and tibialis anterior (TA) muscles (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 decreased the expression of fast MyHC protein in gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior muscles.
source: Further experiments showed that EUG50 and EUG100 increased the expression of slow MyHC and decreased the expression of fast MyHC protein in gastrocnemius (GAS) and tibialis anterior (TA) muscles (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: 12.5–50 μM eugenol boosted slow MyHC expression in C2C12 myotubes.
source: As indicated in Figure 1F, 12.5–50 μM eugenol boosted slow MyHC expression, while 12.5–100 μM eugenol decreased fast MyHC expression.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 12.5–100 μM eugenol decreased fast MyHC expression in C2C12 myotubes.
source: As indicated in Figure 1F, 12.5–50 μM eugenol boosted slow MyHC expression, while 12.5–100 μM eugenol decreased fast MyHC expression.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: High doses (200 μM) of eugenol had no effect on muscle fiber type in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Consistent with our in vivo studies, our in vitro findings again suggested that high doses (200 μM) of eugenol had no effect on muscle fiber type.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1F and H.

claim: EUG100 increased the exhaustion time of mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, EUG100 increased the exhaustion time of mice.
evidence: Supported by exhausting swimming test data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 decreased lactate dehydrogenase activity in the GAS muscle.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, EUG50 and EUG100 decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity and increased succinic dehydrogenase (SDH) activity in the GAS muscle.
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 increased succinic dehydrogenase activity in the GAS muscle.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, EUG50 and EUG100 decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity and increased succinic dehydrogenase (SDH) activity in the GAS muscle.
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EUG100 increased the activities of SDH and malate dehydrogenase in the TA muscle.
source: In the TA muscle, LDH activity was decreased in all EUG groups, and EUG100 increased the activities of SDH and malate dehydrogenase (MDH).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LDH activity was decreased in all EUG groups in the TA muscle.
source: In the TA muscle, LDH activity was decreased in all EUG groups, and EUG100 increased the activities of SDH and malate dehydrogenase (MDH).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The transcript levels of mitochondrial transcription factors Pgc1a, Nrf1, and Tfam were increased in eugenol-treated mice.
source: In addition, the transcript levels of mitochondrial transcription factors Pgc1a, Nrf1, and Tfam and the mRNA expression of components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain were increased in eugenol-treated mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C heatmap.

claim: The mRNA expression of components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain were increased in eugenol-treated mice.
source: In addition, the transcript levels of mitochondrial transcription factors Pgc1a, Nrf1, and Tfam and the mRNA expression of components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain were increased in eugenol-treated mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C heatmap.

claim: The protein expression of mitochondrial electron transport complex I and complex V was upregulated in eugenol-treated mice.
source: The protein expression of mitochondrial electron transport complex I and complex V was upregulated in eugenol-treated mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EUG100 improved the mtDNA copy number in the GAS and TA muscle.
source: Furthermore, EUG100 improved the mtDNA copy number in the GAS and TA muscle (Figure 2E), and 12.5–100 μM EUG increased the mtDNA copy number in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 12.5–100 μM EUG increased the mtDNA copy number in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Furthermore, EUG100 improved the mtDNA copy number in the GAS and TA muscle (Figure 2E), and 12.5–100 μM EUG increased the mtDNA copy number in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both EUG100 and EUG200 promoted average daily feed intake.
source: Our research has found that both EUG100 and EUG200 promoted average daily feed intake (ADF) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by feeding data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Eugenol decreased inguinal white adipose tissue and gonadal white adipose tissue weight.
source: In addition, eugenol decreased inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) weight while promoting brown adipose tissue (BAT) weight (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by tissue weight data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Eugenol promoted brown adipose tissue weight.
source: In addition, eugenol decreased inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) weight while promoting brown adipose tissue (BAT) weight (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by tissue weight data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Eugenol decreased T-CHO and LDL while increasing HDL level in serum.
source: And eugenol decreased T-CHO and LDL while increasing HDL level in serum (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by serum lipid measurement data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Pparg, Hsl, and Fabp4 in iWAT.
source: As we speculated, we found that eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of the fat synthesis-related genes Pparg and Hsl, as well as the fatty acid transport gene Fabp4, in iWAT (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Fasn and Fabp4 in gWAT.
source: In gWAT, it was found that eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of the Fasn and Fabp4 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Cd137, Tbx1, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in iWAT.
source: We further examined the mRNA expression of key genes involved in browning of fat, and found that eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Cd137, Tbx1, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in iWAT, while eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Tmem26, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in gWAT (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Tmem26, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in gWAT.
source: We further examined the mRNA expression of key genes involved in browning of fat, and found that eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Cd137, Tbx1, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in iWAT, while eugenol promoted the mRNA expression of Tmem26, Ucp1, Prdm16, Dio2, and Cidea in gWAT (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Eugenol promoted the expression of the fatty acid transport protein FABP-1 in gWAT.
source: At the protein level, eugenol promoted the expression of the fatty acid transport protein FABP-1, as well as the UCP-1 protein expression in gWAT (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Eugenol promoted the UCP-1 protein expression in gWAT.
source: At the protein level, eugenol promoted the expression of the fatty acid transport protein FABP-1, as well as the UCP-1 protein expression in gWAT (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Eugenol promoted the UCP-1 and PGC-1α protein expression in BAT.
source: It was found that eugenol promoted the UCP-1 and PGC-1α protein expression (Figure 3G), as well as the mitochondrial electron transport complex III and complex V protein expression (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Eugenol promoted the mitochondrial electron transport complex III and complex V protein expression in BAT.
source: It was found that eugenol promoted the UCP-1 and PGC-1α protein expression (Figure 3G), as well as the mitochondrial electron transport complex III and complex V protein expression (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: TRPV1 is expressed in all tissues, including adipose and muscle tissues, with the highest expression in skeletal muscle compared to other TRP channels.
source: Based on the gene expression profiling, it was observed that TRPV1 is expressed in all tissues, including adipose and muscle tissues, with the highest expression in skeletal muscle compared to other TRP channels (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling data from GTEx dataset shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mRNA expression of only Trpv1 was promoted by EUG50 and EUG100 in TA muscle.
source: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis confirmed the expression of TRPV1 and TRPV2 in skeletal muscle, and the mRNA expression of only Trpv1 was promoted by EUG50 and EUG100 in TA muscle.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only Trpv1 mRNA expression was promoted by 25 and 50 μM eugenol in C2C12 cells.
source: In C2C12 cells, only TRPV1-4 were expressed, and only Trpv1 mRNA expression was promoted by 25 and 50 μM eugenol (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: EUG100 and EUG200 promoted Trpv1 mRNA expression in adipose tissue.
source: Adipose tissue expressed TRPV1 and TRPV2 genes, and EUG100 and EUG200 promoted Trpv1 mRNA expression, while EUG50 promoted Trpv2 mRNA expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Eugenol bound at the binding pocket and interacted with THR550, ASN551, LEU553, TYR554, ALA566, ILE569, GLU570, and ILE573 of TRPV1.
source: Moreover, taking the TRPV1-capsaicin binding sites (TYR511, SER512, THR550, and GLU570) (Carnevale and Rohacs, 2016) as the potential binding pocket, molecular docking analysis showed that eugenol bound at the binding pocket and interacted with THR550, ASN551, LEU553, TYR554, ALA566, ILE569, GLU570, and ILE573 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 increased CnA protein expression in the GAS and TA muscles.
source: Our results showed that EUG50 and EUG100 increased CnA protein expression in the GAS and TA muscles (Figure 4D and E), and 12.5–100 μM eugenol promoted CnA protein expression in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: 12.5–100 μM eugenol promoted CnA protein expression in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Our results showed that EUG50 and EUG100 increased CnA protein expression in the GAS and TA muscles (Figure 4D and E), and 12.5–100 μM eugenol promoted CnA protein expression in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The mRNA expression of Mcip1 was increased in EUG100 groups.
source: The regulator of calcineurin 1 (MCIP1) is a biomarker to reflect the CaN activity (Yang et al., 2000), the mRNA expression of Mcip1 was increased in EUG100 groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The nuclear translocation of NFATc1 was promoted by EUG50 and EUG100 in the GAS and TA muscles.
source: Furthermore, the nuclear translocation of NFATc1 was promoted by EUG50 and EUG100 in the GAS and TA muscles, and by 12.5–50 μM eugenol in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data of nuclear protein shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The nuclear translocation of NFATc1 was promoted by 12.5–50 μM eugenol in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Furthermore, the nuclear translocation of NFATc1 was promoted by EUG50 and EUG100 in the GAS and TA muscles, and by 12.5–50 μM eugenol in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data of nuclear protein shown in Figure 4I.

claim: TRPV1 inhibition weakened the increase in intracellular Ca2+ levels induced by eugenol.
source: The results showed that TRPV1 inhibition weakened the increase in intracellular Ca2+ levels induced by eugenol, suggesting that eugenol acts via TRPV1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN attenuated the effect of eugenol on CaN.
source: Furthermore, the inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN attenuated the effect of eugenol on CaN (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Eugenol increased the mitochondrial electron transport complex I, II, III, and V protein expression.
source: In addition, eugenol increased the mitochondrial electron transport complex I, II, III, and V protein expression, the inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN attenuated the effect of eugenol on complex I, III, and V (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN attenuated the effect of eugenol on complex I, III, and V.
source: In addition, eugenol increased the mitochondrial electron transport complex I, II, III, and V protein expression, the inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN attenuated the effect of eugenol on complex I, III, and V (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Eugenol promoted the fast-to-slow muscle fiber transformation, while the inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN eliminated this effect.
source: Importantly, immunofluorescence and western blot analysis revealed that eugenol promoted the fast-to-slow muscle fiber transformation, while the inhibition of TRPV1 and CaN eliminated this effect (Figure 5D and Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: A23187 increased the mRNA expression of MCIP1.
source: As shown in Figure 6A–C, A23187 increased the mRNA expression of MCIP1, the protein expression of CnA, and CaN activity.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A23187 increased the protein expression of CnA.
source: As shown in Figure 6A–C, A23187 increased the mRNA expression of MCIP1, the protein expression of CnA, and CaN activity.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A23187 increased CaN activity.
source: As shown in Figure 6A–C, A23187 increased the mRNA expression of MCIP1, the protein expression of CnA, and CaN activity.
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 0.5 μM A23187 increased intracellular Ca2+ levels.
source: We chose 0.5 μM A23187 for subsequent experiments and confirmed that it increased intracellular Ca2+ levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A23187 significantly increased the mRNA expression of Fndc5, Il6, Il15, and Metrnl.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, A23187 significantly increased the mRNA expression of Fndc5, Il6, Il15, and Metrnl.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E heatmap.

claim: Il13 mRNA expression was not detected in C2C12 myotubes.
source: However, Il13 mRNA expression was not detected in C2C12 myotubes.
evidence: This is a negative result from the qPCR experiment.

claim: The highest correlation coefficient (R=0.954) was between Mcip1 expression and Il15 expression.
source: In addition, a correlation heatmap showed the highest correlation coefficient (R=0.954) between Mcip1 expression and Il15 expression, followed by Mcip1 and Il6 (R=0.846), Mcip1 and Metrnl (0.77), and Mcip1 and Fndc5 (0.651) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TFBS prediction revealed more potential binding sites between the Il15 promoter and NFATc1.
source: Furthermore, a TFBS prediction revealed more potential binding sites between the Il15 promoter and NFATc1 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics prediction shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Treatment with 0.5 and 1 μM Ca2+ ionophore led to upregulation of IL-15 protein expression.
source: Firstly, it was observed that treatment with 0.5 and 1 μM Ca2+ ionophore led to upregulation of IL-15 protein expression (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ca2+ ionophore treatment upregulated the expression of CnA, NFATc1, and IL-15 proteins.
source: We found that Ca2+ ionophore treatment upregulated the expression of CnA, NFATc1, and IL-15 proteins, while inhibition of CaN eliminated these effects (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Inhibition of CaN eliminated the effects of Ca2+ ionophore on CnA, NFATc1, and IL-15 protein expression.
source: We found that Ca2+ ionophore treatment upregulated the expression of CnA, NFATc1, and IL-15 proteins, while inhibition of CaN eliminated these effects (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Ca2+ ionophore treatment increased the expression of slow MyHC and decreased the expression of fast MyHC.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ ionophore treatment increased the expression of slow MyHC and decreased the expression of fast MyHC, while CsA blocked this effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CsA blocked the effect of Ca2+ ionophore on MyHC expression.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ ionophore treatment increased the expression of slow MyHC and decreased the expression of fast MyHC, while CsA blocked this effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A sequence (5'-AATGGAAAA-3') in the promoter regions of IL-15 was predicted as a potential binding site of NFATc1.

claim: EUG100 promoted Il15 mRNA expression in EDL and SOL muscle.

claim: The mRNA expression of Il15 was higher in SOL muscle than in EDL muscle.

claim: EUG50 and EUG100 increased the concentration of IL-15 in the serum.

claim: IL-15 was a oxidative muscle fiber type-specific myokine that was promoted by eugenol.

claim: TRPV1 assembles as tetramers to form cation-permeable pores.
source: TRPV1, like all other TRP channels, assembles as tetramers to form cation-permeable pores (Clapham, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clapham, 2003.

claim: TRPV1 was initially identified as a capsaicin receptor and heat-activated ion channel that modulates pain and neurogenic inflammation.
source: Initially identified as a capsaicin receptor and heat-activated ion channel that modulates pain and neurogenic inflammation (Caterina et al., 1997), subsequent studies have found that TRPV1 is expressed on many non-neural sites and plays roles in immunity, vasculature, obesity, and thermogenesis (Fernandes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caterina et al., 1997.

claim: TRPV1 is expressed on many non-neural sites and plays roles in immunity, vasculature, obesity, and thermogenesis.
source: Initially identified as a capsaicin receptor and heat-activated ion channel that modulates pain and neurogenic inflammation (Caterina et al., 1997), subsequent studies have found that TRPV1 is expressed on many non-neural sites and plays roles in immunity, vasculature, obesity, and thermogenesis (Fernandes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernandes et al., 2012.

claim: Capsaicin activated TRPV1 to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism.
source: Previous studies have also shown that capsaicin activated TRPV1 to improve endurance capacity and energy metabolism (Luo et al., 2012), counter obesity (Baskaran et al., 2016), and intervene diabetes (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2012.

claim: 50 and 100 μM eugenol promoted TRPV1 expression in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found that eugenol activates TRPV1 in a heterologous expression system and rat trigeminal ganglion neurons (Xu et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003), and a recent study reported that 50 and 100 μM eugenol promoted TRPV1 expression in C2C12 myotubes (Jiang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2022.

claim: Capsaicin-induced TRPV1 activation was shown to promote exercise endurance and the skeletal muscle oxidative phenotype.
source: In a previous study, capsaicin-induced TRPV1 activation was shown to promote exercise endurance and the skeletal muscle oxidative phenotype (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: TRPV1 activated calmodulin-dependent protein kinase by increasing intracellular Ca2+, and the activation of CaMK further activated PGC-1α.
source: The authors suggested that TRPV1 activated calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CaMK) by increasing intracellular Ca2+, and the activation of CaMK further activated PGC-1α, contributing to these effects (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: CaN induces the translocation of NFATc1 to the nucleus by dephosphorylating NFATc1, thereby switching fast-to-slow muscle fibers.
source: CaN induces the translocation of NFATc1 to the nucleus by dephosphorylating NFATc1, thereby switching fast-to-slow muscle fibers (Calabria et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calabria et al., 2009.

claim: TRPV1 activation has been shown to promote CaN activity in several other cells and tissues.
source: TRPV1 activation has been shown to promote CaN activity in several other cells and tissues (Hou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2018), but the link between TRPV1 and CaN signaling in skeletal muscle has not yet been established, nor has it been determined whether TRPV1 promotes muscle oxidative phenotype through the CaN/NFATc1 signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Eugenol increases muscle glucose uptake through the TRPV1/CaMK signaling pathway.
source: Recent studies have also found that eugenol increases muscle glucose uptake through the TRPV1/CaMK signaling pathway (Jiang et al., 2022), suggesting that both CaN and CaMK signaling may be involved in TRPV1-facilitated skeletal muscle oxidative phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2022.

claim: An increase in slow-twitch fiber content is positively associated with reduced obesity and improved metabolic health.

evidence: Supported by citation to Carlson et al., 2010.
